method: Retain all four original independent English essays and their 14-block structures. Local factual corrections, necessary source-attribution qualifications, and one restored title close reading; no wholesale retranslation or Chinese-English block equality requirement.

corrections.before: The second part of We Three is called “The Three of Us Are Separated.” Zhongshu is taken away in a vehicle for an unexplained meeting. Yang Jiang and their daughter search until she reaches an old post road governed by peculiar rules: an inn admits her for one night only; questions are useless; each day she walks to a boat where Qian Zhongshu lies; she must leave before dark. The next day the boat has moved farther on, so the walk lengthens. Their daughter falls ill inside another dream, and eventually the boat departs beyond reach. This can sound like an allegorical interruption in an otherwise lucid memoir. Read beside the family’s chronology, however, it looks less invented than reported. The road reproduces the shape of Yang’s days.
corrections.after: The second part of We Three is called “The Three of Us Are Separated.” Zhongshu is taken away in a vehicle for an unexplained meeting. Yang Jiang and their daughter search until she reaches an old post road governed by peculiar rules: she follows visible paths, does not ask about what she does not know, and returns to an inn by sunset; each day she walks to a boat where Qian Zhongshu lies; she must leave before dark. The next day the boat has moved farther on, so the walk lengthens. Their daughter falls ill inside another dream, and eventually the boat departs beyond reach. This can sound like an allegorical interruption in an otherwise lucid memoir. Read beside the family’s chronology, however, it looks less invented than reported. The road reproduces the shape of Yang’s days.
reasons: Dream rules do not limit each inn to one night.

corrections.before: Qian Zhongshu entered hospital in 1994. The next year Qian Yuan, their only daughter, was admitted to another hospital. Yang Jiang, already in her eighties, travelled between the two, caring for each while concealing the seriousness of the other’s illness. Qian Yuan died in 1997; Qian Zhongshu followed in 1998. The post road translates that routine without reducing it to diagnosis. Its rule against asking resembles the helplessness of medical waiting: one seeks an answer that no answer can make usable. The nightly return resembles visiting hours. The boat moving farther away gives physical distance to decline. The inn that never permits a second night captures the absence of any place where the carer may finally stop. These are not decorative symbols placed over experience. They are the experience’s working timetable.

Remove invented one-night rule; retain author interpretation.

corrections.before: Near the end of the dream, Yang calls the family’s home an inn on a journey. The phrase can be generalized into a reflection on transience, but the memoir gives it material force. The family lived in rented Oxford rooms, cramped Shanghai quarters, institutional housing in Beijing, a borrowed office and finally the Sanlihe apartment assigned through work. They moved repeatedly and owned none of these places in the ordinary sense. Their home therefore could never be identified securely with property. A room became home when the three occupied it through breakfast, books, teasing and conversation; after Qian Yuan and Qian Zhongshu were gone, the same walls reverted to being rooms. “Inn” is both literal and existential. Buildings sheltered them temporarily. The durable form was a relation, and no deed could preserve that form after two of its members disappeared.
corrections.after: Near the end of the dream, Yang calls the family’s home an inn on a journey. The phrase can be generalized into a reflection on transience, but the memoir gives it material force. They moved repeatedly during their shared life. The continuity of home lay not in any one building but in the people living together. A room became home when the three occupied it through breakfast, books, teasing and conversation; after Qian Yuan and Qian Zhongshu were gone, the same walls reverted to being rooms. “Inn” draws force from those repeated moves as well as from the dream. Buildings sheltered them at different stages. The durable form was a relation, and no deed could preserve that form after two of its members disappeared.
reasons: Do not claim lifelong absence of property; preserve home-as-people argument.
No unsupported literal-property proof.

corrections.before: The book begins with two pages titled “The Two of Us Grow Old.” Yang dreams that she and Zhongshu are walking together; he vanishes into dusk, she searches and calls, and then wakes. He tells her that old people often have such dreams. This recoverable loss prepares the unrecoverable one in the second part. Only after separation has been completed does the long third part return to the family’s earlier life. The order reverses conventional memoir. Instead of letting affection accumulate until death supplies a climax, Yang announces at the outset: they are gone; I am alone. Every amusing mishap and ordinary meal is then read under knowledge of its ending. The structure is severe, but it is also faithful to the writer’s position. At ninety-two she does not remember forward in innocence. She looks backward from a room in which every remembered day already contains its disappearance.
corrections.after: The book begins with two pages titled “The Two of Us Have Both Grown Old.” Yang dreams that she and Zhongshu are walking together; he vanishes into dusk, she searches and calls, and then wakes. At ninety-two she does not remember forward in innocence. She looks backward from a room in which every remembered day already contains its disappearance.

corrections.before: In Oxford in 1935, soon after their marriage, Qian Zhongshu woke before Yang Jiang and attempted breakfast: toast, warm milk, an egg and tea, carried upstairs on a large tray. Yang remembered it as the most fragrant breakfast she had eaten. The experiment became an arrangement. Zhongshu made breakfast through Oxford, the return to China, Shanghai, Beijing and the decades that followed, until illness stopped him in his eighties. In the social world they inhabited, domestic work by a celebrated male scholar could appear undignified; acquaintances noticed. The couple did not reorganize their morning to satisfy that judgment. The act did not make Zhongshu a better comparatist or produce another volume of scholarship. It made a shared day begin in a particular way. Repeated for a lifetime, a small impropriety became part of the household’s constitution.
corrections.after: In their early Oxford days, soon after their marriage, Qian Zhongshu woke before Yang Jiang and attempted breakfast: toast, warm milk, an egg and tea, carried to her bed on a large tray. Yang remembered it as the most fragrant breakfast she had eaten. The experiment became an arrangement. Zhongshu regularly made breakfast through Oxford, the return to China, Shanghai, Beijing and the decades that followed. Yang specifies exceptions: periods in an extended-family household, periods when a maid prepared their meals, and his illnesses. In the social world they inhabited, domestic work by a celebrated male scholar could appear undignified; acquaintances noticed. The couple did not reorganize their morning to satisfy that judgment. The act did not make Zhongshu a better comparatist or produce another volume of scholarship. It made a shared day begin in a particular way. Repeated across decades, a small impropriety became part of the household’s constitution.
reasons: Breakfast occurs around New Year; no need to fix it to 1935.
No unsupported downstairs/upstairs route.
Book explicitly states three exceptions; preserve long habit.
Same continuity qualification.

corrections.before: The private language kept multiplying. Husband and wife gave one another nicknames; together they named their daughter. When Qian Yuan was small, her father drew a comic face on her stomach after she fell asleep. She woke protesting, and he did it again. As an adult she traded teasing notes with him. Because she lived at some distance, one would leave a scrap on the table, the other answer, and the exchange continue with reports of foolish behaviour and affectionate mockery. They kept the stacks. The memoir also remembers meal after meal: improvised cooking in Oxford, shortages in Shanghai, shopping and cooking in Beijing, Qian Yuan coming home to eat. These details occupy more room than public milestones. They do not educate the child in any measurable skill, improve the family’s position or become art outside the household. They are acts whose audience and beneficiary are the same three people.
corrections.after: The private language kept multiplying. Husband and wife gave one another nicknames; together they named their daughter. When Qian Yuan was small, her father drew a comic face on her stomach after she fell asleep. His mother scolded him, and he did not dare repeat it. As an adult she remained a companion in teasing. Family letters and remembered jokes preserve reports of foolish behaviour and affectionate mockery, small traces of their daily life. The memoir also remembers meal after meal: improvised cooking in Oxford, shortages in Shanghai, shopping and cooking in Beijing, Qian Yuan coming home to eat. These details occupy more room than public milestones. They do not educate the child in any measurable skill, improve the family’s position or become art outside the household. They are acts whose audience and beneficiary are the same three people.
reasons: Original prank is one summer incident, not recurring after daughter protests.
Remove unverified distant-residence/table-relay/stacks combination without replacing private-language argument.

corrections.before: The absence of use becomes striking once we recall who spent the time. Qian Zhongshu wrote Fortress Besieged, Limited Views and scholarship almost no one else could have produced. Yang Jiang became a writer and translator, learning Spanish in middle age before completing her major translation of Don Quixote. Qian Yuan was a respected professor and builder of an English programme. This was a household capable of treating every hour as scarce professional capital. Instead, its members spent large quantities of attention on imagined strangers, private jokes and notes no outsider needed to read. They did so not because work was easy or time abundant. The great books and translations were produced under punishing conditions. Uselessness occupied the intervals deliberately left unconverted. Those intervals were not failed productivity. They were the portion of life that did not have to justify itself through an output.

corrections.before: When Yang Jiang reaches 1966, she records that both she and Qian Zhongshu were subjected to the humiliating half-shaved hairstyle of the period. Her practical response was to recover hair cut from earlier years, combine it with some of her own and make a wig she could wear to buy groceries. When Zhongshu was sent to a cadre school in Henan and Yang followed, she writes about cultivating vegetables and the walks they could take when their assignments brought them within reach. After returning, they lacked housing and stayed in an office; later they moved books yet again. The facts are not softened. Public humiliation, forced labour, separation and professional interruption are all present. What surprises is the scale of the prose. The wig can sound ingenious, the vegetables become specific, and the catastrophe is not granted a rhetorical climax.
corrections.after: In her separate memoir Bingwu Dingwei Nian Jishi, Yang Jiang records their humiliation in 1966. A cross was shaved into Qian Zhongshu’s hair, and she later shaved the rest clean; she herself was subjected to a half-shaved head. Her practical response was to make a wig from her daughter’s saved braid, using her husband’s hair cap as its base and a small pot as a form. We Three recalls Zhongshu going to a cadre school in Henan and Yang following the next year. In the separate Six Chapters from My Life Downunder, she writes about the vegetable garden and their brief encounters there, keeping attention on daily work and ways of meeting. After returning to Beijing they moved several more times, temporarily staying in an office in 1974; the books moved with them. The facts are not softened. Public humiliation, forced labour, separation and professional interruption are all present. What surprises is the scale of the prose. The wig can sound ingenious, the practical details remain specific, and the catastrophe is not granted a rhetorical climax.
reasons: Correct haircut subjects/materials and explicitly identify other memoir; do not invent this book’s garden vignette.
Do not collapse the later office stay into immediate post-cadre-school homelessness.
Keep tone analysis after removing unverified vegetable details.

corrections.before: Yang does not hide the shaved heads, denunciations, false accusations, banishment, lost work or absence of a home. Evasion would require removing the events or disguising their effects. Her selectivity operates elsewhere. She rarely assigns blame, names an offender or expands an incident into a judgment on the age. That silence remains open to criticism; acknowledging her formal choice does not make every consequence beyond debate. Yet it matters that she withholds evaluation rather than evidence. The distinction changes the question. Why would a writer capable of analysis leave the public verdict outside this family memoir? Because once the campaigns become the organising subject, the household becomes an example. Breakfast, notes and walks are demoted to “warmth amid suffering,” valuable mainly for illustrating the cruelty of history. Yang refuses that hierarchy. The private life is not a footnote to the disaster. It is the book’s principal reality.
corrections.after: Yang does not hide suffering. We Three records denunciations, false accusations, banishment, interrupted work and insecure accommodation; the separate memoir supplies the detailed account of the shaved heads and wig. The distinction changes the question. Why would a writer capable of analysis leave the public verdict outside this family memoir? Because once the campaigns become the organising subject, the household becomes an example. Breakfast, notes and walks are demoted to “warmth amid suffering,” valuable mainly for illustrating the cruelty of history. Yang refuses that hierarchy. The private life is not a footnote to the disaster. It is the book’s principal reality.
reasons: Do not attribute every cross-text detail to We Three.

corrections.before: The quietness is best understood as proportion. Political campaigns occupy relatively few pages; meals, books, teasing, errands and conversations occupy most of them. This is not a claim that the campaigns were harmless or brief. It is a claim about the total composition of lived time. A denunciation can dominate historical meaning without filling every hour of the day. People still eat, sleep, cultivate a plot, exchange a scrap of paper and look forward to a walk. Yang uses the words anxiety and loneliness for the cadre-school period; she does not deny suffering. She then records that the couple met at the edge of the vegetable ground and continued talking. The conjunction matters. Misery was real, and so was the rest of life. By controlling the page ratio, she prevents the most coercive force in their environment from becoming the sole author of what those years were.
corrections.after: The quietness is best understood as proportion. Political campaigns occupy relatively few pages; meals, books, teasing, errands and conversations occupy most of them. This is not a claim that the campaigns were harmless or brief. It is a claim about the total composition of lived time. A denunciation can dominate historical meaning without filling every hour of the day. People still eat, sleep, cultivate a plot, exchange a scrap of paper and look forward to a walk. A passage in Six Chapters from My Life Downunder makes the relation concrete. Zhongshu’s quarters were a little over ten minutes from Yang’s vegetable garden. Serving as a messenger to the post office, he would later often pass the plot. They sat briefly in the sun on the bank of the channel or stood talking; he handed her letters written in fragments. Anxiety and loneliness are not erased, but the narrative continues with what they did within those conditions. The conjunction matters. Misery was real, and so was the rest of life. By controlling the page ratio, she prevents the most coercive force in their environment from becoming the sole author of what those years were.
reasons: No unverified exact phrase or garden dialogue attributed to this book; preserve conjunction and proportion analysis.

corrections.before: During years when scholarship, friendship and thought had to be explained through approved purposes, the family preserved activities for which no form had a box. Inventing a passer-by’s biography, writing nonsense to a daughter, reading different books in one room and preparing breakfast for one’s wife did not serve an institution. They survived partly because they were too small to classify. Yang notes that Zhongshu declined opportunities for advancement and continued pursuing recondite textual work whose utility to the moment was nearly impossible to state. She writes of this in the same register as his household mishaps. The equality of tone is deliberate: neither the scholarship nor the joke needs public necessity to become worthwhile. What totalising systems seek to remove from a person is often precisely this surplus beyond function. We Three restores page after page of that surplus.
corrections.after: During years when scholarship, friendship and thought had to be explained through approved purposes, the family preserved activities for which no form had a box. Inventing a passer-by’s biography, writing nonsense to a daughter, reading different books in one room and preparing breakfast for one’s wife did not serve an institution. They survived partly because they were too small to classify. Yang notes that Zhongshu declined some appointments but also reluctantly accepted a nominal post: after resigning as an adviser to the Institute of Literature in 1982, he became a vice-president of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. His resignation a year later was not accepted; he continued to draw a researcher’s salary and kept reading and research at the centre of his life. His recondite textual work scarcely answered the demands of immediate utility. She writes of this in the same register as his household mishaps. The equality of tone is deliberate: neither the scholarship nor the joke needs public necessity to become worthwhile. What totalising systems seek to remove from a person is often precisely this surplus beyond function. We Three restores page after page of that surplus.
reasons: Not a lifelong refusal of all office; retain noninstrumental reading without false premise.

corrections.before: Qian Yuan died in 1997 and Qian Zhongshu less than a year later. Yang Jiang remained in the Sanlihe apartment for another eighteen years and died at 105. She wrote We Three at ninety-two, five years into that solitude. The intervening life was not empty. She sorted sacks of Zhongshu’s reading notes—Chinese and foreign excerpts, annotations and associations in difficult handwriting—into published volumes. The work continued for more than a decade, with later instalments appearing after she had passed one hundred. She translated, wrote Reaching the Brink of Life in her mid-nineties and used the couple’s royalties to establish a scholarship. Organising marginalia could neither restore its author nor greatly increase his reputation. It was the last large-scale version of the family’s useless acts: caring for the traces of another person’s attention because they were what he had left.

Organising marginalia could neither restore its author nor greatly increase his reputation. It was the last large-scale version of the family’s useless acts: caring for the traces of another person’s attention because they were what he had left.

corrections.before: Yang gives a modest explanation: she wanted to set down the days when the three were together. She does not claim to provide a national testimony, a model household or the definitive memorial to two eminent intellectuals. The inventory confirms the scale. An Oxford breakfast, biographies invented on a walk, a painted face on a child’s stomach, foolish scraps of paper, spilled ink, a broken lamp, a damaged hinge and the repeated assurance that it could all be mended. A ninety-two-year-old who had just lost husband and daughter chose these details over public honours. Their smallness is not camouflage for a grander subject. It is the subject. By writing them one after another, Yang gives durable form to events whose original value lay precisely in not needing an audience beyond the three people present.

corrections.before: At the end Yang says their home was only an inn on the road and that she is still searching for the way home. Read abstractly, the lines may sound like a lament about the vanity of earthly attachment. The family’s housing history makes them more concrete. Oxford rooms were rented, Shanghai quarters borrowed, Beijing accommodation institutional and Sanlihe assigned. No building possessed an uninterrupted claim to be theirs. The home existed when the relations did. It accumulated through mornings, reading, cooking, teasing, errands and returns. Take away two people and the apartment remains, but the form called home does not. Yang’s search is therefore not for another property or even for a metaphysical answer the memoir could supply. It names the impossibility of locating in space what had always been made through the presence of three particular lives.
corrections.after: At the end Yang says their home was only an inn on the road and that she is still searching for the way home. The home existed when the relations did. It accumulated through mornings, reading, cooking, teasing, errands and returns. Take away two people and the apartment remains, but the form called home does not. Yang’s search is therefore not for another property or even for a metaphysical answer the memoir could supply. It names the impossibility of locating in space what had always been made through the presence of three particular lives.
reasons: Avoid universal property claim; preserve narrow home relation point.

corrections.before: The title is not My Husband and Daughter, Remembering Qian Zhongshu or Sixty Years of a Family. “We three” is household speech, an informal name the members used for themselves. Yang places that phrase on the cover after she has become the only living speaker. The grammatical subject of the book is therefore not the survivor alone. Conventional mourning often takes the form “I suffer,” “I lost” or “this was the greatness of the dead.” Yang gives loss its dream in the opening sections, then allows the plural to govern most of the pages. When she remembers Zhongshu’s incompetence with a lamp or Qian Yuan’s teasing, the tone recovers pleasure because the event itself was pleasurable. Grief does not retroactively change the emotional truth of what happened. The singular writer can still testify to a plural past.
corrections.after: The third part is titled “I Alone Remember We Three”: in its nine Chinese characters, “I alone” names the present, “we three” the shared decades, and “remember with longing” joins them. corrections.before: Across four essays, the pattern comes together. A long dream captures two years during which each day lengthened the road toward separation. The remembered decades are filled with acts that produced nothing: a scholar makes breakfast, three readers share a room, family members invent strangers, trade nonsense and preserve paper scraps. History presses for complete accounts of a person’s use; the household keeps what cannot be accounted for. Yang’s quiet tone records injury without surrendering the scale of memory to it. Finally, the survivor asks where home is and cannot locate it because home was never the building. It was the relation named by the book. “I alone remember we three” holds singular and plural in one sentence without resolving their contradiction. One person remains. Three people performed those days. The task of the one is not to replace the three, but to keep their completed life from being rewritten solely as absence.
